sections.overview: Wild lions now survive in fragmented parts of sub-Saharan Africa and in one Asian population in western India. They use settings from savanna and scrub to dry woodland, while prey and human pressures vary between regions. In India, lions move through the wider Gir landscape, where protected forest meets farms and settlements.
sections.identification: The lion has a muscular, deep-chested body, a short tawny coat, pale underparts and a long tail tipped with a dark tuft; cubs often have fading spots. Adult males usually grow a mane whose length and shade vary with age and individual; females generally lack one. African reference adults average 180 kilograms and 1.20 metres at the shoulder for males, and 130 kilograms and 1.05 metres for females; individuals vary. Asiatic lions often have shorter manes and a more visible abdominal fold. Retractile claws grip prey; long canines kill and cheek teeth slice meat. For comparison across references, the Smithsonian reports shoulder heights of about 1.0–1.2 m; males may reach 3 m in body length plus a 0.6–0.91 m tail and weigh 150–250 kg, while females may reach 2.7 m and weigh about 120–179 kg. These are broad zoo-reference values, while the regional averages above describe African populations.
sections.habitat: Lions occupy savannas, grasslands, scrub, open woodland and dry forests, provided that cover, prey and relatively undisturbed den sites are available. Gir combines dry deciduous forest, thorn scrub, grassland and river corridors within a cultivated regional landscape. Asiatic lions may rest in dense vegetation by day and range more widely at night, sometimes near farms and settlements. A comparison across ten habitats found that seasonal food scarcity, rather than overall prey abundance alone, was linked to larger home ranges.
sections.diet: Lions are opportunistic carnivores, but medium and large hoofed mammals usually supply most of their food. They stalk close before a short rush, then use jaws and forelimbs to bring prey down. Group hunts may divide roles, but observations show that participation varies and some lions hang back when prey is easier to catch. In Gir, chital, sambar, nilgai and wild pigs are documented prey; livestock made up a larger share of recorded kills in peripheral areas than inside the protected landscape.
sections.behavior: In many African populations, a pride is a flexible, fission-fusion group built around related females and their young. Males may hold territory in coalitions, while females often stay in their birth group and young males disperse; local patterns vary. Pride members split into smaller parties and reunite to rest, care for cubs, mate or defend territory. Both sexes roar and growl to communicate. Roars maintain contact with pride members and advertise territorial boundaries; lions can use the number of callers they hear to assess the strength of rivals. At Gir, female groups and male coalitions commonly use separate ranges, meeting mainly to mate or at large kills.
sections.reproduction: Females breed in different seasons; gestation lasts about 110 days and litters usually contain one to four cubs. A mother gives birth in a secluded thicket, hiding the cubs for their first weeks and returning to nurse them. Cubs eat meat from about three months and are weaned near six months, yet Gir young may depend on the natal group for food until two or three years old. Females may first breed at about three and a half years; males often mate only after securing territory. A takeover by unfamiliar males can put cubs at risk; mothers may hide or defend them, and outcomes vary with age and local conditions.
sections.ecology: Food scarcity can enlarge territories and reduce prides: a comparison of ten habitats linked lean-season prey availability with group size and cub survival. Lions consume large herbivores, but also compete with other carnivores over carcasses, scavenging and sometimes losing kills to rivals. In Gir, the balance between wild prey and livestock shifts with season and location, linking prey access to local feeding patterns.
sections.conservation: The IUCN global assessment, made on 1 February 2023 and published in 2024, lists lions as Vulnerable and the trend as decreasing. It inferred a 36 percent range reduction over three generations, with habitat loss, prey depletion and conflict-related killing among the pressures. African populations are fragmented; Gujarat’s protection and habitat management have supported a recovery, but India’s lions remain concentrated in one regional population. The government reported 891 Asiatic lions in its 2025 count on 10 August 2026.
